excerpt: Switch from TeamViewer, AnyDesk, and Splashtop to RustDesk for a secure and reliable remote desktop experience with your own self-hosted servers.

Personalize RustDesk client with your name, icon, logo.
More than 90 options can be configured to meet your specific needs.
Host the web client on your server with your domain name to make remote access even easier.
Works on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, Web.
Supports VP8 / VP9 / AV1 software codecs, and H264 / H265 hardware codecs.
P2P connection with end-to-end encryption based on NaCl.
No administrative privileges or installation needed for Windows, elevate privilege locally or from remote on demand.
Remote view and control, unattended access with a permanent password, file transfer in both directions, in-session text chat, and session recording.

A user noted that under Wayland, RustDesk offered a "Fix it!" button that ran sed on gdm system config files to revert to X11. They also said the code had almost no comments and lots of unexplained `unsafe`, and they would keep it off their machines.

A user tried RustDesk as a TeamViewer alternative to help their dad, but it refused to install on his older macOS version. The website didn't make supported OS versions clear, so it took a lot of effort before ending in disappointment.

After two years with AnyDesk and its growing ads and 'pro use' prompts, a user switched to RustDesk: "This is really great. I dare say the performance is 'better' than anydesk," though they admitted it wasn't measured objectively.

A user complained that RustDesk seemed to require a relay server and couldn't connect directly by IP. Self-hosting needed a license that wasn't on sale, and with the default server being slow, it was "unusable."

Awesome on the first try on Ubuntu 18.04 LTS and Mac. It recognized two screens, let the user click 1 or 2 to choose which to show, and has a shrink feature to fit a bigger remote screen on the local display.

"RustDesk works so much better and easier than vnc and other vendored solutions. No need to open ports, no need for vpn, it just works, no account BS, no vendor lock in." The user has used it for years with their own lookup/relay server.

Self-hosting the server forces zero authentication, so anyone can use it for free. The user has to run it through a VPN, which hurts performance and latency and makes it unusable as an easy IT help tool. The paid Pro version has authentication.

A daily user said RustDesk has been a nice alternative/replacement for AnyDesk; they use both 10+ times a day. They had trouble getting remote desktop working on an Orange Pi 5 and welcomed the Wayland unattended-access fix.
Microphone input passthrough from client to host is the only feature this user found missing compared to proprietary solutions.
Tried it with my mom, but it would freeze after 15 seconds of shared session time.

A user drives RustDesk 12 hours a day on up to 9 computers and finds it visually much better than AnyDesk. It has no NumLock bug and can play YouTube where AnyDesk chugs. However, alt-tab has issues from Linux to Windows 10, and file copy-paste from Linux to Windows doesn't work.

An AUR package co-maintainer said it "doesn't work very well or reliably," the developer is almost impossible to communicate with, CI is poor, and it's nearly impossible to self-host. They're forced to keep using AnyDesk.
A user self-hosted the server with Docker and it seemed to work. You point the Windows client to the server via the .exe filename, but they warned that encryption is not enabled by default.
A user uses RustDesk to remote into a Mac Mini from Windows machines and says it is very good, whereas VNC is awful on Macs unless used from another Mac.
A user praised RustDesk's community as very active and its developers as "VERY VERY responsive to all questions."
It was extremely laggy and nearly impossible to connect. After installing the Docker server on their own machine, the user got the same result and found it unusable.
Trying to connect from an Android tablet to a PC caused the tablet to hard reboot.

A user who replaced AnyDesk with RustDesk uninstalled it after reading about the security issues and that relay servers may be hosted in Beijing. They were uncomfortable with the ambiguity for software that opens access to their whole system.
Over RustDesk installing a test certificate in the Windows root store, a user removed their self-hosted RustDesk server and the clients from all their devices until the situation is clarified.

A user disputed RustDesk's driver-signing justification for the root certificate. They said kernel-mode drivers need Microsoft cross-signing anyway, and the normal approach is to generate a local CA and destroy its private key afterward.
